title: The Good Parts of an Order
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
Danse wrote DO NOT FORCE A CROSSING at the top of the emergency checklist.

Then he stared at the sentence for a long time.

"Too strong?" I asked.

"No."

He tapped the page.

"Not strong enough."

We were working in Brasswatch Yard, where the emergency planning group had gathered after the generator failure and the storm at Tideglass. The lower service passage remained sealed. The repaired upper gate had not yet passed its final test. People needed a reliable way to find shelter or return home when the weather made ordinary routes unsafe.

The old emergency manual was full of instructions that assumed someone with a uniform could decide what happened to everyone else.

Danse had already removed the section about identifying untrustworthy visitors by their origins.

Now he was looking at the parts that said travelers should be moved through the nearest available Threadway regardless of preference.

"That's not how our doors work," I said.

"I know."

He looked at the paper.

"But in an emergency, there may not be time for a long discussion."

Katara, who was reviewing the medical section, put down her pen.

"Then the procedure should make the questions simple before the emergency happens."

Neri nodded.

"People can choose a preferred shelter or ask for a private departure plan in advance. We don't need to record why they choose it."

Edda raised a hand.

"And the route has to be one people can actually use. A safe arch is not a safe evacuation route if the path to it has three steps and no alternative."

Danse began writing.

We built the checklist around decisions that could be made quickly without stealing anyone's agency. First, identify immediate danger. Second, announce the available routes and their known conditions. Third, ask which option the person wants. Fourth, provide assistance only with consent, except for the narrow circumstances in which someone cannot respond and there is an immediate threat to life.

Even those exceptions required a written review afterward.

It was less tidy than a chain of command.

It was better.

Renn, now working as a training assistant, tested the instructions by pretending to be a frightened newcomer with a suitcase.

Danse approached.

"The lower path is closed. The ridge route is open, and the hall has shelter. Would you like help getting there?"

Renn shook their head.

"I want to go through the east Threadway."

Danse glanced at the map.

"That route is safe at present. I can show you the way."

Renn looked surprised.

"That's it?"

"That's it."

"What if I won't tell you where I'm going?"

"You don't have to."

Renn smiled.

"Good."

Then Edda tested a different scenario.

"What if I can't use the ridge because the gravel is loose?"

Danse looked at the route sheet.

"We have a level alternate path marked in blue."

"And if it's flooded?"

"Then we tell you. We don't conceal the risk to make the plan look complete."

She nodded.

"Now we're getting somewhere."

We ran six scenarios before lunch. In one, a child was separated from their caregiver. In another, a visitor declined assistance despite a safe shelter being available. In a third, someone wanted to remain in a secure home rather than join the crowd at the hall.

Not every scenario had a neat answer.

That was the point.

By afternoon the checklist had grown shorter. We removed phrases that required volunteers to interpret someone's loyalty, intentions, or worthiness. We replaced them with clear conditions and choices.

Danse looked exhausted.

"You're frowning," I said.

"I'm remembering how many times I used to give orders without asking what they cost."

I sat beside him.

"You can keep the useful skills."

He looked at me.

"Can I?"

"Organization. Clear signals. Knowing how to keep people safe. None of those belong to the Brotherhood forever."

He thought about that.

"Then perhaps the good parts of an order are the parts that help someone choose."

I smiled.

"Write that down."

He did.

We posted the final draft for public feedback. It wasn't approved immediately. Tamsin wanted the structural instructions reviewed. Katara requested more detail on medical assistance. Edda asked for the map to be available in multiple formats. Neri wanted the privacy rules explained in plain language.

Danse accepted every comment.

A year ago, I thought he might have interpreted that as an attack.

Today he thanked them.

That evening we walked through the yard while the lanterns came on. The generator hummed quietly behind the workshop, operating within its posted load limit.

"May I ask something?" he said.

"Of course."

"Do you feel safe with me?"

I stopped.

It would have been easy to say yes immediately and use the word as a blanket over everything difficult.

Instead I thought about the doors he'd learned to leave open, the mistakes he'd admitted, and the ways we had negotiated time and privacy without pretending love meant ownership.

"I feel safe asking you to change," I said. "And I feel safe telling you when something isn't right."

He looked at me.

"That means more than I expected."

I took his hand.

"Do you feel safe with me?"

He considered.

"Sometimes I'm still frightened you'll find my history too heavy."

"I know."

"But I don't feel required to hide that fear from you."

I leaned closer.

"Good."

He kissed me beneath the workshop sign, warm and gentle. The repaired light above the door made a small circle of gold around us.

In the morning, Renn arrived with another suggestion.

The checklist needed a section for people who chose not to disclose personal information to volunteers.

Danse added it without complaint.

There was always another useful question.
